Reading a Part Number Like an Engineer

The 11 characters of 25N125HLS-Z spell out diameter, thread type, length, head style and finish. Just as telling is what the number leaves out: no leading period, so it’s inch series, and no material letter, so it’s plain steel.

Topic T2 · Part Number Decoder

Five Key Part Characteristics

Hover over any element of the part number below to see what it means — the same way SBS Engineering reads a new item, one piece at a time.

25N125HLS-Z  =  1/4 X 1 1/4 HEX LAG SCREW ZINC
What the Number Leaves Out

No Leading Period = Inch

Metric SBS part numbers start with a “.”. This one starts straight with a digit, so it is an inch-series part — the E-Catalog confirms: Measurement System, Inch (English).

No Material Letter = Steel

There is no “S” for stainless. When a part number does not call out a material, the reasonable assumption is plain steel — and the item specification confirms it.

What Makes a Lag Screw a Lag Screw

Built for Wood

Lag screws are commonly used in wood construction — heavy timber, decks, ledger boards, brackets — wherever a bolt and nut can’t reach the back side.

Gimlet Point

A sharp cone point, about 60° per the ASME drawing, that centers in a pilot hole and starts the thread. No nut is ever used.

Sharp Cutting Thread

Coarse and widely spaced — 10 TPI on a 1/4″ lag. The thread cuts its own mating thread in the wood as it is driven.

External Hex Drive

The hex head takes a wrench or socket, so a lag can be driven with far more torque than a slotted or Phillips wood screw.

Topic T4 · Material Selection

Plain Steel

There is no material letter in 25N125HLS-Z. Here’s how to read that — and why the finish matters so much on this part.

Requirement

Material: Steel · Grade: Steel · Finish: Zinc (Cr3)

Reading the Silence

When a part number or description doesn’t state a material, a reasonable assumption is plain steel — about 90% of the world’s fasteners are steel. A stainless part would carry an “S” in its part number.

“Grade: Steel”

The grade field simply repeats “Steel”. No strength grade is called out, which is typical for lag screws: they are rated by how they hold in wood, not by a bolt-style strength class.

Cost

Plain steel is the economical choice. A stainless lag of the same size would typically cost two to four times more.

Weakness: Rust

Bare steel rusts quickly outdoors or in damp wood. That is the job of the zinc plating called out by “-Z”.

Where Stainless Wins

In treated lumber, marine or wet service, a stainless lag is usually the better call — the zinc layer is thin and is consumed over time.

Why It Matters

Recognizing a steel part from its number tells you to look for a finish call-out next. Steel with no finish is rarely what a customer wants.

See how the zinc layer protects the steel in .

Topic T5 · Zinc (Cr3) Finish

Zinc Plating with a Trivalent Passivate

The “-Z” at the end of the part number calls out the finish. The E-Catalog spells it out: Zinc (Cr3).

Requirement

Finish: Zinc (Cr3). Electroplated zinc, followed by a trivalent chromium (Cr3) passivate.

How You Spot It

A bright silver finish with a faint blue tint — the look of every lag screw in the sample photo.

Item E3 as received: the bright zinc (Cr3) finish.
What Zinc Plating Actually Does
  • Sacrificial protection. Zinc corrodes before steel does. Even where the coating is scratched, the surrounding zinc keeps protecting the steel underneath.
  • A thin layer. Electroplated zinc is only a few microns thick — enough for indoor or sheltered use, not for long outdoor or marine exposure.
  • The passivate seals it. A chromium conversion layer over the zinc slows white rust (zinc corrosion) and gives the finish its color.
  • No thread-fit worries here. On a machine screw, plating thickness eats into thread clearance. A lag screw cuts its own thread in wood, so that’s not a concern.
The SBS Finish Guide
Click the image to enlarge.
The SBS Finish Guide entry for zinc: codes, plating thickness, Cr3 vs. Cr6 conversion, salt-spray hours and RoHS status. Coatings and Finishes | Specialty Bolt & Screw Inc. ↗
Cr3 vs. Cr6: Why the “(Cr3)” Matters

Cr3 — Trivalent

The modern passivate. It contains no hexavalent chromium, so it meets RoHS and similar restrictions. Usually clear or bluish.

Cr6 — Hexavalent

The older chromate (classic gold or yellow zinc). Hexavalent chromium is a restricted hazardous substance, and many customers no longer accept it.

Reading a Finish Call-Out

“Zinc” alone is incomplete. Always check which passivate (Cr3 or Cr6) and which color the customer expects.

Hydrogen Embrittlement

Plating can trap hydrogen in hardened steel and cause cracking. Plain, low-strength steel like this lag screw is at very low risk.

Topic T6 · ASME B18.2.1 Table 15

Reading the Lag Screw Table

This is a standard part: its dimensions are set by ASME B18.2.1, not by a customer print. Table 15 holds every hex lag screw size — ours is the 1/4 row.

The Standard Itself
Click the image to enlarge.
ASME B18.2.1-2012 (R2021), Table 15 — Dimensions of Hex Lag Screws. Read the full ASME B18.2.1 standard ↗
  1. E — Body diameter: 0.237–0.260″ for the 1/4 size.
  2. F — Width across flats: 7/16″ basic, 0.425–0.438″.
  3. G — Width across corners: 0.484–0.505″.
  4. H — Head height: 11/64″ basic, 0.150–0.188″.
  5. S and R — shoulder length 0.094″ min, fillet radius 0.01–0.03″.

Reference

Glossary

Every code, acronym, and standard used in this module, defined in plain language. Tap a term's "jump" button to see it in context.

ASME B18.2.1

The ASME standard for inch-series square, hex, heavy hex and askew head bolts and hex, heavy hex, hex flange, lobed head and lag screws. Table 15 holds the hex lag screw dimensions.

BRP

Bombardier Recreational Products — one of SBS’s customers. This item carries BRP customer part number 250000119.

Confirm COO

A P21 flag requiring the country of origin to be confirmed when the item is received.

Cr3 (Trivalent Chromium)

The modern chromium passivate applied over zinc plating. Unlike Cr6 (hexavalent), it is not a restricted hazardous substance.

Gimlet Point

A sharp, cone-shaped screw point (about 60°) that starts its own thread in wood. Standard on lag screws.

Inspection Template

A controlled blank form, linked to the item in P21, that lists each feature to check, its tolerance and the inspection method.

Lag Screw

A heavy wood screw with a hex (or square) head, coarse sharp thread and gimlet point, driven with a wrench into wood. No nut is used.

P21

SBS’s ERP system (Epicor Prophet 21), where items, documents, suppliers and inventory are maintained.

PPAP

Production Part Approval Process — the documentation package a supplier submits to prove its process can reliably make a part to specification. Level 4 means a PSW plus whatever else the customer defines.

RoHS

Restriction of Hazardous Substances — an EU rule limiting materials such as lead, mercury and hexavalent chromium in manufactured parts.

Track Lots

A P21 flag that records the vendor lot of every receipt, so parts can be traced back to their source.

TPI

Threads per inch. This 1/4″ lag screw has 10 TPI, a 0.100″ thread pitch.

Width Across Flats / Corners

The two key hex head sizes: across flats (F) sets the wrench size; across corners (G) is the widest point of the hex.

Zinc Plating

An electroplated zinc layer that protects steel by corroding first (sacrificial protection). Called out by “-Z” in the part number.
